query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding a ductilizing element such as niobium (Nb) to an HfZrTi high-entropy alloy will improve its ductility and toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An equimolar HfZrTi high-entropy alloy that is intrinsically strong but brittle, showing limited ductility and toughness.
generation.intervention: Alloying the HfZrTi system with a controlled amount of Nb to form an HfZrTiNb alloy.
generation.conditions: Standard laboratory processing conditions with subsequent mechanical testing at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Niobium atoms incorporated into the matrix, leading to a more favorable distribution of atomic bonding and potential for activating additional slip systems.
generation.mechanism: Nb, as a subgroup V transition metal, is expected to enhance solid‐solution strengthening in a manner that reduces brittleness and promotes dislocation mobility, thereby relieving stress concentrations at the grain boundaries or phase interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HfZrTiNb HEA should show a measurable increase in tensile ductility and fracture toughness relative to the base HfZrTi alloy.
generation.baseline: Pure HfZrTi high-entropy alloy without Nb addition.
generation.boundary: Excessive Nb content might lead to the formation of undesired brittle phases, so there is an optimal range for Nb addition.
generation.uncertainty: The precise improvement in ductility and toughness and the optimal Nb concentration require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one set of equimolar HfZrTi alloy and another set with a targeted Nb addition (forming HfZrTiNb) at various concentrations. Perform standardized tensile and fracture toughness tests at both room and elevated temperatures, while characterizing the microstructure using TEM and SEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HfZrTiNb samples do not show statistically significant increases in ductility and toughness compared to the baseline HfZrTi, or if Nb addition results in the formation of brittle intermetallic phases that compromise mechanical properties, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
